name: DEXA body fat scan

lead: A DEXA scan gives you a measured body fat percentage and a map of fat and lean mass by region. People use it to find out how lean they actually are, which shapes whether they cut or bulk for a sharper physique and face.

Two X-ray beams of different energies are absorbed differently by bone, fat and lean tissue, and software separates them. It was developed mainly for bone density and osteoporosis. Reference sources describe its body composition accuracy as comparable to hydrostatic weighing and strongly correlated with MRI and CT.

paras: People book a scan at a clinic or imaging center, often before starting a cut or bulk and again after several weeks or months to see the change. Many go at the same time of day, with similar hydration and the same machine, so repeat readings can be compared. Forum members often cite a DEXA figure to confirm they are lean enough before considering fat-reduction procedures.

Radiation from modern machines is very low. Lean-mass readings shift with hydration, table size and weight limits apply, about 40 percent of pixels can't be classified where soft tissue overlaps bone, and different manufacturers' scanners give different numbers, so readings from different machines are not directly comparable. It is a measuring tool, not a treatment.

web.title: The Pitfalls of Body Fat Measurement, Part 6: Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DEXA)
AI-powered body composition scans: can they actually monitor health risk?

angle.text: A DEXA scan shows your real body fat and lean mass by region, so you can decide whether to cut or bulk toward a leaner look. It is a medical imaging method chiefly studied for bone density; its use for physique tracking comes from forum practice.

lead: A DEXA (also written DXA) scan is a low-dose X-ray test that passes beams at two energy levels through the body and uses the difference in absorption to separate bone from soft tissue. It was built for bone mineral density testing and is the most widely used technology for diagnosing and monitoring osteopenia and osteoporosis; the same scan can also report whole-body and regional fat mass and lean mass.[1][2]

For appearance, the scan is a measuring tool that tells people how lean they are and where their mass sits. Lifters and physique-minded members use it to check a body-fat figure before choosing whether to cut, maintain or build; to see whether a training block added lean mass while fat fell; and to look at regional fat, which matters for people trying to bring out facial angles, jawline and abdominal definition through fat loss.[3][4][5]

Researchers regard DEXA as reproducible on the same machine and well correlated with MRI and CT, while noting that its fat and lean estimates depend on assumptions about tissue hydration, differ between manufacturers, and are less certain for an individual's change over time than for group averages.[1][6][7][2] Scans are available from hospitals and, in the United States, from consumer scanning services, and the method is also used as the body-composition endpoint in drug trials.[8][7]

paras: A DEXA scanner emits X-ray beams at two energy levels. Because bone and soft tissue attenuate the two energies differently, the soft-tissue contribution can be subtracted to quantify bone mineral. Where pixels contain no bone, the software estimates the ratio of fat to lean soft tissue.[1]

For body composition the machine reports whole-body totals and regional results, up to 14 body areas according to Wikipedia's body-composition article, and can produce a low-resolution fat-shadow image of overall fat distribution.[2][1] The test is fast and non-invasive.[2]

Standard bone-density reports give areal density (mass per area) rather than true volumetric density, one reason results can overestimate bone density in taller or larger-boned people and underestimate it in smaller-boned people.[1]

DEXA's established role is in osteoporosis care. The US Preventive Services Task Force recommends DXA screening for women over 65, and the World Health Organization defines T-score thresholds for postmenopausal women.[1]

Body-composition research with the technique goes back decades. A study that began in December 1989 as a collaboration with Russian colleagues scanned 18 cosmonauts before and after 4 to 14.4 months on the Mir station, measuring bone and lean-tissue loss; it was published in 2000.[9]

Newer milestones include a 2025 Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology substudy that used DXA-measured total fat mass as the primary endpoint in a phase 2 trial of retatrutide,[8] and an FDA decision, dated 19 December 2025 on Wikipedia, to qualify total hip bone mineral density from DXA as a surrogate endpoint in osteoporosis drug trials.[1]

sections.h: Use in appearance and physique contexts

paras: Because it separates fat from lean tissue, DEXA gives a more detailed body-fat figure than a scale or skinfold reading. Wikipedia notes its use in fat-distribution and lipodystrophy assessment.[1] Forum members describe getting a scan to establish a baseline before a cut or a bulk; one T Nation post describes taking a scan to see a starting point before a contest prep.[10]

A looksmax.org reply advises confirming a sub-10 percent body-fat figure with a DEXA before consulting a clinic about ultrasound cavitation, treating the scan as the check on whether further fat reduction is needed.

Lifters post before and after scans to show changes in lean tissue and fat. Examples on T Nation include a member reporting a drop from 18.2 to 16.3 percent body fat across eight months with lean tissue up 1.7 lb, and another reporting a drop in body-fat percentage over eight months with a rise in lean mass, both attributed to their own scans.[5][4]

Other members use a single scan as a reality check. A 23-year-old poster reports a scan showing 31 percent body fat after years of training, and a post about a scan result of 10 percent is listed among one member's yearly goals.[11][3]
One member describes a US scan costing about 40 dollars and taking about 5 minutes; this is an individual forum report rather than published price data.[10]

Facial leanness is part of why body-fat measurement appears in looksmaxxing discussions: members connect lower overall body fat with more visible jaw and cheekbone structure. DEXA reports regional body fat rather than facial fat specifically, and whole-body figures are what members usually cite.[2]

Wikipedia describes DXA body-composition accuracy as comparable to hydrostatic weighing and strongly correlated with MRI and CT, and lists limitations: lean mass depends on hydration status, there are table size and weight limits, about 40 percent of pixels (those where soft tissue overlaps bone) cannot be measured, and some studies find biases when measuring changes in fat mass.[1] Scanners from different manufacturers can give significantly different results, so cross-calibration is recommended.[1]

James Krieger, writing on Weightology, summarises comparisons with a four-compartment model: group-average errors of about 1 to 2 percent but larger individual errors, with one study reporting about 4 percent and another 8 to 10 percent. He reports that a 5 percent variation in fat-free-mass hydration can shift DEXA body-fat percentage by nearly 3 percent, and that software upgrades and fan-beam geometry can change results. He suggests spacing scans at least 3 to 6 months apart when tracking change.[6]

Steven Heymsfield of Pennington Biomedical Research Center says DEXA is the most accessible reference option and is usually used for validation studies, but is two-dimensional and needs several assumptions; he and Cyrus Raji describe MRI as the most accurate method for visceral fat and lean tissue, though costly.[7] Wikipedia's body-composition article notes that DEXA is highly reproducible on the same machine, which makes it useful for tracking, and that some researchers question its use as a criterion measure.[2]

The four-compartment model, which combines body weight, density, total body water and DEXA mineral, is described there as the reference standard, with some sources calling DEXA alone the gold standard.[2] Interpretation of the bone-density use also has caveats: degenerative spine changes can inflate readings, and misreading of children's scans has been linked to overdiagnosis of osteoporosis in children.[12][13]

Wikipedia's body-fat-percentage article lists alternatives: underwater weighing (about plus or minus 3.8 percent uncertainty even when done perfectly), air displacement plethysmography, near-infrared interactance, bioelectrical impedance (cheap but affected by hydration, eating and exercise) and skinfold calipers (which measure only subcutaneous fat and depend on technique).[14]

In an Athletech News piece, Raji says bioelectrical impedance is the most widely available option and that camera-based apps currently lack scientific validity compared with clinical tools; a Frontiers in Nutrition study cited there found one impedance device read about 3 percent lower than DEXA but was reliable day to day.[7] A vendor-reported accuracy for one camera app is described in the article as a company claim.[7]

Modern DEXA systems deliver a very small radiation dose, as low as about 0.001 mSv, lower than a standard chest or dental X-ray; older radioisotope-based systems delivered higher doses.[1] Wikipedia's body-composition article says exposure is lower than a cross-country flight.[2]

DEXA is a measurement method rather than an appearance intervention, so no trials test it as a treatment. It is widely used as the measurement in other studies. Examples include the Mir cosmonaut study of bone and lean-tissue loss,[9] the retatrutide substudy that used DXA total fat mass as its primary endpoint,[8] and comparisons of DEXA T-scores against CT-derived bone measures.[12]
For its use as a tool in looksmaxxing, no studies specific to that setting were found.

Members of looksmax.org mention DEXA as the benchmark for body fat, sometimes advising that a confirmed low body-fat reading come before considering procedures such as ultrasound cavitation. On T Nation, scans appear in training logs and transformation threads as a way to show progress, with members posting percentages and lean-mass changes after cuts and bulks.[3][4][5][15]
Posters also compare methods; one member mentions having done hydrostatic body-fat testing years earlier for a college class and says it may be time to repeat a measurement.[15]

lore.intro: Within looksmaxxing and lifting forums DEXA is referenced as the accurate way to know body fat, usually as a precondition before fat-loss decisions or as a progress check after a cut or bulk.[5]

claims.claim: A DEXA scan is the way to confirm your real body-fat percentage.
Repeat DEXA scans show whether you are gaining lean mass and losing fat.
DEXA readings from different scanners are interchangeable.
Hydration and prep do not change the result.
Cheap home tools such as smart scales or camera apps match a DEXA scan.
The radiation from a body-composition scan is a concern.
